extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy-makers, and practitioners involved in grant peer review (NIH reviewers, study section chairs, research policy scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical description of how NIH-style study sections evaluate R01-type grant applications, including scoring rubric, reviewer roles, meeting workflow, triage, and discourse practices that influence scoring (e.g., Score Calibration Talk). Useful for designing, studying, or improving grant peer review panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse nine-point scoring rubric (NIH)
rubrics_metrics.description: At NIH, reviewers employ a reverse nine-point scale, with each number corresponding to a single descriptive adjective (Figure 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each numeric score maps to an adjective (e.g., 'exceptional', 'outstanding'), but the precise meaning of adjectives (what distinguishes 'exceptional' vs 'outstanding') is left ambiguous so reviewers apply expert judgment. Ambiguity in criteria increases subjectivity and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five core review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers evaluate applications based on five criteria: significance, investigator qualifications, innovation, methodological approach, and research environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigned reviewers provide preliminary scores for each of the five criteria and an overall (overall impact) score; critiques should address strengths and weaknesses across these criteria; these criteria form the basis for justification of numerical scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written critique requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are responsible for reading each application assigned to them and writing a thorough critique of the application's strengths and weaknesses, including a holistic impression of the overall impact of the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should provide accounts that justify scores; public accounting (verbalized rationale during meeting) enables establishment of common ground. The study treats written critiques as pre-meeting inputs that inform preliminary scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three assigned reviewers per application (primary/secondary/tertiary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each application has three assigned reviewers in a given panel meeting designated primary, secondary, and tertiary based on relevance of reviewers' expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRO assigns designations; the primary reviewer has the most relevant expertise and typically leads the summary; these three provide preliminary scores that determine which applications are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary scoring and SRO averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The three assigned reviewers provide preliminary scores prior to the meeting; the SRO calculates the average preliminary score across the three assigned reviewers for each application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRO uses average preliminary scores to determine order of review (strongest first) and which applications are discussed (top 50%). Preliminary scores are the independent reviewers' baseline and are used to compute triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage: top 50% discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the top 50% of applications, based on average preliminary score, are discussed during the meeting; the bottom half are 'triaged' from discussion and not considered further for funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triage procedure directly affects which applications receive panel discussion and final scores; panels may differ substantially in which applications are triaged depending on preliminary scoring variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting workflow and score-reporting sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: During panel meetings the SRO provides opening remarks and reviews scoring, the chair introduces the application, the three assigned reviewers state their preliminary scores (the 'score-reporting sequence') and summarize their critique, chair opens discussion, then chair summarizes and calls for final scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'score-reporting sequence' is a formalized step; how reviewers present scores and rationales (order, framing) can influence ensuing discussion and score change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final scoring and expectation about score range
rubrics_metrics.description: After discussion the three assigned reviewers publicly announce their final scores; the lowest and highest of these constitute the 'score range' for the application. Non-assigned panelists privately record final scores expected to fall within the range; if outside, they must announce and may provide rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are as many final scores as panel members; Final Panel Score is the average of these individual scores multiplied by 10 (range 10–90). The expectation that non-reviewers' scores fall within the range enforces a norm but allows declared divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Panel Score calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Panel Score is the average of all panelists' scores (i.e., the three assigned reviewers plus all non-reviewing panelists) multiplied by 10 (such that Final Panel Scores range from 10 to 90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Panel Scores are used by NIH governance to inform funding decisions; multiplication by 10 converts the 1–9 scale to 10–90 for administrative use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to disclose any institutional or other conflicts of interest with an application, as is standard NIH practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is required prior to review to manage potential bias and to inform SRO/chair decisions about participation in discussion or scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-identification of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications were de-identified with names replaced and identifying information altered or removed to reduce effects of prior knowledge of applicants or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-identification aims to reduce bias stemming from reputation or prior knowledge; reviewers were instructed to refer only to provided materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assignment and load norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical reviewer rosters and assignment loads: standing study sections often have 18–21 reviewers with assignments of ~9–10 applications; ad hoc panels/SEPs might have 8–10 reviewers and assignments as low as 5–6 applications; CSS panels in study targeted 12 reviewers and assigned each reviewer six applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel size and reviewer load influence time available per application and may affect discussion depth and scoring outcomes; videoconference meetings may be smaller with lesser reviewer loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section officer (SRO) and chair roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO oversees the study section, determines order of review, assigns reviewers, and provides opening remarks. The chair introduces applications, moderates discussion, summarizes critiques, and calls for final scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRO and chair shape meeting structure and enforcement of norms (e.g., time, score reporting); consultations with SRO/CSR guided CSS design to simulate NIH practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-per-application guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings were timed to ensure panel spent approximately 15 minutes reviewing each application, creating time pressure similar to actual NIH study sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time constraints approximate real-world conditions and can shape the extent and character of discussion and opportunities for score calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score Calibration Talk (SCT) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Score Calibration Talk is discourse in which reviewers make explicit references to the scoring habits of fellow panelists; it is a form of discourse related to grounding the meaning of numeric scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCT is identified as a pivotal interactional mechanism that influences scoring variability; the study identified 71 instances across panels and analyzed its role in establishing common ground around what numbers mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-initiated SCT (S-SCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: S-SCT: any instance during which reviewers mention their scores (either the word 'score' or the number itself) along with an account (rationale or justification) for that score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accounting of one's scoring rationale allows others to access and potentially adopt that interpretive frame; merely stating 'I gave it a four' without rationale is not S-SCT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other-initiated SCT (O-SCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: O-SCT: any instance in which one panelist calls on other reviewers to account for their scoring practices by offering a 'challenge' to their score (e.g., known-answer questions or solicitations that function as challenges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O-SCT can be brief or extended multi-speaker exchanges (e.g., 'Your comments are meaner than your score'); O-SCT operates as an interactional pressure that can elicit clarification or change in scoring behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding methodology for SCT instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcripts were exhaustively coded for any instance of discourse related to scores or scoring norms; two coders inductively evaluated instances, timed seconds spent on each instance, and resolved discrepancies collaboratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding reliability procedures included independent coding and team adjudication for start/stop times; small number of SCT instances required discussion to resolve timing discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability measurement using Krippendorff’s alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-rater and inter-panel agreement were quantified using Krippendorff’s α; values above 0.80 considered 'reliable' and values between 0.67 and 0.80 considered suitable for tentative conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports extremely poor inter-reviewer reliability for preliminary scores (α ≈ 0.084) and changes in α intra-panel (preliminary -> final reviewer -> final panel). Krippendorff’s α accommodates multiple raters and missing values and is recommended for these analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of evaluative adjectives as a quality risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Because descriptive adjectives linked to numeric scores are left ambiguous, judgments become susceptible to subjectivity and bias when criteria are not specifically defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that ambiguous criteria can be locally grounded by panels (local interpretations) which may increase inter-panel variability; thus, clarifying criteria may reduce unwarranted subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of panelists' scoring behavior (norm enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-reviewing panelists' final scores are expected to fall within the range defined by the three assigned reviewers; deviations should be announced and can be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This norm functions as an accountability mechanism shaping convergence within panels, and is part of the procedural rules intended to produce consistent Final Panel Scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of constructed study sections (CSS) to simulate real study sections
rubrics_metrics.description: CSS method: recruit experienced NIH reviewers, de-identify applications, use SRO and NIH staff consultation, assign reviewers in NIH-like fashion, videotape meetings, and simulate timing and procedures to approximate real study section behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (panel size, reviewer load, videoconference inclusion) were made to resemble NIH practice and to permit observation of real-time discourse; participant surveys confirmed high similarity to real NIH study sections.
